narrative:
The model estimated that you have a 72.5% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt, and that risk estimate is why your law school application was denied. In practical terms, the decision treated failure as substantially more likely than success, so your application did not proceed.

Your third-year class standing was the strongest factor. You are in the lowest decile (1.00) in your school based on Year 3 grades, while accepted students averaged around decile 5.79. That comparatively low standing pushed the prediction strongly toward bar failure. Your first-year standing was the second most important factor: you were also in decile 1.00 then, versus an accepted-student average near 6.00, and this also increased the estimated failure risk. The third factor, your undergraduate GPA of 3.50, worked in your favor: it is above the accepted-student average of 3.23 and pushed the prediction toward passing, but it was not enough to offset the two class-standing signals.

To improve future applications, focus on strengthening the academic indicators weighed most heavily here, especially sustained improvement in law-school grades and class standing. Meet with an academic advisor to build a plan, retake the LSAT only if practice indicates a meaningful gain, and apply to schools or programs where your profile is a closer match. You may also ask admissions offices what updated evidence they accept.
